nodes.title: Apply Newton's first law to bodies in equilibrium
nodes.canonical_question: How does Newton's first law describe a body at rest or moving at constant velocity when the net force is zero?
nodes.summary: Newton's first law: with zero net force a body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity. To apply it, list the forces, check they balance, and conclude the motion is unchanging.

nodes.title: Identify inertial reference frames
nodes.canonical_question: What is an inertial reference frame, and how can you tell whether Newton's first law holds in a given frame?
nodes.summary: An inertial frame is one in which a body with no net force keeps constant velocity. Accelerating or rotating frames are non-inertial; in them objects seem to move with no real force.

nodes.title: The book on the table: balanced forces
nodes.canonical_question: Why does a book resting on a table not fall through even though gravity pulls it down?
nodes.summary: Gravity pulls the book down, but the table pushes up with a normal force of exactly equal size. The table’s surface compresses very slightly under the book, like a stiff spring, and pushes back just hard enough to balance the weight.

nodes.title: Why resting objects stay put
nodes.canonical_question: Why does an object sitting on a surface stay still if gravity acts on it?
nodes.summary: A resting object is not free of forces; it has gravity and the surface’s support pulling and pushing in opposite directions. The surface supplies exactly the upward force needed to cancel gravity, no more and no less.

nodes.title: What makes a frame inertial
nodes.canonical_question: What actually makes a reference frame inertial?
nodes.summary: A reference frame is inertial if an object with no net force on it moves in a straight line at constant velocity when viewed from that frame. A lab bench at rest on the ground is very nearly inertial for everyday purposes.

nodes.title: Recognizing inertial frames
nodes.canonical_question: How can you recognize whether a given reference frame is inertial?
nodes.summary: To check a frame, imagine a body with zero net force and watch how it moves in that frame. The ground is a good enough inertial frame for a game of billiards.

nodes.title: Why equilibrium means zero net force
nodes.canonical_question: Why does mechanical equilibrium require the net force to be exactly zero?
nodes.summary: The first law says motion changes only when a net force acts, so a body whose motion is not changing must feel zero net force. Zero net force means the forces cancel in every direction at once, not just up and down.

nodes.title: Why Earth is nearly inertial
nodes.canonical_question: Why can Earth’s surface be treated as an approximately inertial frame despite its rotation?
nodes.summary: Earth rotates and orbits, so strictly its surface is a non-inertial frame. Over large scales or long times the rotation shows up, for instance in the swing of a Foucault pendulum or the curving of winds.

nodes.title: The first law at constant velocity
nodes.canonical_question: How does Newton’s first law apply to a car cruising at constant velocity?
nodes.summary: A car holding a steady speed in a straight line has zero net force, even though its engine is working. Press the accelerator and the drive force exceeds resistance, so a net force appears and the car speeds up.

nodes.title: Fictitious forces in accelerating frames
nodes.canonical_question: What fictitious forces appear in a non-inertial (accelerating) reference frame?
nodes.summary: In an accelerating frame, objects seem to be pushed by forces that have no physical source. Pressed back into your seat as a car accelerates, or flung outward on a roundabout, you feel such apparent forces.

nodes.title: Tension in a rope at rest
nodes.canonical_question: How do you find the tension in a rope holding a hanging weight at rest?
nodes.summary: A weight hanging still from a rope is in equilibrium, so the upward tension exactly balances the downward weight. If a 2 kg mass hangs at rest, its weight is about 20 N, so the rope tension is about 20 N.
